title: Stripes on the seafloor
teaches: How magnetic reversals recorded in ocean-floor rock showed the sea floor spreading apart

blocks.text: In 1955 the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey ship Pioneer spent months sailing back and forth off the coast of California, Oregon and Washington, mapping the depth of the sea floor for the Navy. Scientists from the Scripps Institution of Oceanography arranged to tow a magnetometer behind it, an instrument that measures the strength of the Earth's magnetic field. Because rocks containing iron minerals are slightly magnetic themselves, the field at the sea surface is a little stronger over some rocks and a little weaker over others.

When Ronald Mason and Arthur Raff drew up the results in 1961, the pattern was strange. Bands of stronger and weaker field ran roughly north to south, each a few kilometres to a few tens of kilometres wide and up to hundreds of kilometres long, like the stripes on a zebra. Some bands were offset sideways along east-west lines, as if the sea floor had been cut and shifted. No one could explain them.

blocks.caption: The sea floor off Washington and Oregon, shaded the same way as the land; the coast runs down the right third of the map. The red line follows the Juan de Fuca Ridge, which runs down the middle of the striped area.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Magnetic surveys off the Pacific Northwest found long, parallel stripes of stronger and weaker magnetic field in the sea floor.

blocks.text: The rock of the ocean floor is **basalt** (lesson 4), and basalt contains small grains of **magnetite**, a magnetic iron oxide. While the lava is hot, the magnetism of those grains is scrambled. As it cools below about 580 °C, each grain's magnetism freezes in line with the Earth's field at that moment, and stays that way. A lava flow is a fossil compass, recording which way north was when it cooled.

Early in the twentieth century, geologists found something unexpected in such rocks. In 1906 the French physicist Bernard Brunhes found lavas in central France magnetised in the opposite direction to the present field, pointing south instead of north. In 1929 Motonori Matuyama found the same in lavas in Japan, and noticed that the reversed rocks were all older than the normal ones. The explanation, slowly accepted, is that the Earth's magnetic field itself flips: every so often, the north and south magnetic poles trade places.

The field is generated by molten iron flowing in the Earth's outer core, and the flow is turbulent enough that the field occasionally collapses and rebuilds the other way round. The intervals between flips are irregular, from tens of thousands to millions of years. In the early 1960s two groups, Allan Cox, Richard Doell and Brent Dalrymple in California and Ian McDougall and Don Tarling in Australia, dated lava flows from around the world by their radioactive potassium and recorded each flow's magnetic direction. The result was a timescale of reversals: the last flip was about 780,000 years ago, and before that the field was mostly reversed for nearly two million years, with brief normal intervals.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Cooling lava locks in the direction of the Earth's magnetic field.
The field reverses at irregular intervals; the last reversal was about 780,000 years ago.
Dated lava flows on land give a timescale of reversals.

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the American geologist Harry Hess had proposed in 1962 what Robert Dietz named **seafloor spreading**. Hess suggested that the long ridges in the middle of the oceans are places where hot mantle rock rises, partly melts, and erupts as new basalt crust. The new crust moves away on both sides, carried by the slow flow of the mantle, and the ocean widens. Somewhere else, old ocean floor must sink back into the mantle, because the Earth is not getting any bigger.

In 1963 Fred Vine, a graduate student at Cambridge, and his supervisor Drummond Matthews put the two ideas together. If new crust forms at a ridge and spreads away while the magnetic field flips, then each strip of crust would record the field's direction at the time it cooled. The sea floor would be striped in bands of normal and reversed magnetisation, parallel to the ridge, the same on both sides, like a tape recording running outward in both directions. Normal bands add to today's field and reversed ones subtract from it, which is what a ship's magnetometer would see. Lawrence Morley in Canada had the same idea independently, but two journals turned his paper down.

blocks.caption: A spreading ridge. New crust takes on the direction of the field (dark: normal, as today; pale: reversed) and moves away on both sides. Top: the magnetic field a ship would measure; the dotted line is a survey to match.
blocks.task: Find the spreading rate that matches the survey

blocks.text: This idea makes two predictions. The stripes should be symmetrical about the ridge, and their widths should be proportional to the lengths of time in the reversal timescale, stretched by the spreading rate. In 1965 and 1966 both predictions were confirmed. Vine and the Canadian geologist J. Tuzo Wilson matched the stripes over the Juan de Fuca Ridge, in the middle of Raff and Mason's survey, to the timescale. Walter Pitman, at Lamont Geological Observatory in New York, produced a profile across the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge from the research ship Eltanin so symmetrical that it convinced many doubters on sight. It even showed a short normal interval, now called the Jaramillo, that had only just been found in lavas on land.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: New ocean crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and spreads away on both sides.
Magnetic stripes are symmetrical about the ridge and match the reversal timescale.
Stripe width divided by time gives the spreading rate, a few centimetres a year.

parts.title: The age of the ocean floor

blocks.text: The stripes let geologists date the ocean floor without drilling it. Once the reversal timescale was extended back in time, every stripe in every ocean could be assigned an age, and maps of the age of the sea floor followed. They show young crust along the ridges and older crust toward the edges of the oceans, exactly as spreading requires.

In 1968 the drilling ship Glomar Challenger tested this directly. It drilled through the sediment on the floor of the South Atlantic at sites progressively farther from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, and dated the oldest sediment resting on the basalt at each site from its microfossils. The ages increased steadily away from the ridge, as the magnetic stripes predicted.

blocks.caption: Spreading rates, counting both sides of the ridge, compared with familiar speeds.

blocks.text: The oldest ocean floor anywhere is about 180 million years old, in the western Pacific. Continents contain rock up to four billion years old; the ocean floors are all young, which means that ocean floor is constantly being destroyed as well as made. The Atlantic is still widening by about the length of a finger every year, carrying the Americas away from Europe and Africa, which is how Wegener's continents move: they ride along on the spreading plates rather than ploughing through the ocean floor. Where the old sea floor goes is the subject of the next lesson.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Ocean floor gets older away from the ridges, as confirmed by drilling in 1968.
No ocean floor is older than about 180 million years, so old ocean floor must be destroyed somewhere.
Continents move because they are carried along by spreading plates.

blocks.caption: Five questions on seafloor spreading
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: How does a basalt lava flow record the direction of the Earth's magnetic field?
choices: Magnetite grains lock in the field's direction as the lava cools below about 580 °C
The lava flows in the direction of magnetic north
Iron settles to the north side of the flow
items.why: Above about 580 °C the magnetism of magnetite is scrambled; on cooling it freezes in line with the field.

items.ask: Why are the magnetic stripes the same on both sides of a mid-ocean ridge?
choices: Crust formed at the ridge is split and carried away equally in both directions
The Earth's field is stronger on one side of the ridge
The stripes were made by currents flowing along the ridge
items.why: Each strip of new crust records the field as it cools, then moves off to one side or the other, so the two sides are mirror images.

items.ask: A stripe 1.8 million years wide in the timescale is 54 km wide on one side of a ridge. What is the spreading rate on that side?
items.why: 54 km in 1.8 million years is 30 km per million years, which is 30 mm or 3 cm a year.

items.ask: What did the Glomar Challenger find when it drilled sites at different distances from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
choices: The oldest sediment at each site got older with distance from the ridge
The sediment was the same age everywhere
The sea floor was oldest at the ridge
items.why: Sediment starts to settle on new crust as soon as it forms, so the oldest sediment dates the crust beneath, which ages away from the ridge.

items.ask: Why is no ocean floor older than about 180 million years, when continents contain much older rock?
choices: Ocean floor is destroyed elsewhere as fast as it is made at the ridges
The oceans only formed 180 million years ago
Older ocean floor has been buried under continents by erosion
items.why: The Earth is not growing, so as new sea floor forms at ridges, old sea floor must sink back into the mantle somewhere.

learned: Cooling basalt records the direction of the Earth's magnetic field, which reverses at irregular intervals.
New ocean floor forms at mid-ocean ridges and spreads away symmetrically, recording reversals as magnetic stripes.
Stripe widths and the reversal timescale give spreading rates of a few centimetres a year.
Ocean floor is young, at most about 180 million years old, so it must be destroyed somewhere.
